newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jerusalem bombs delay U.S. peace moves.
newsitem.headline: Jerusalem bombs delay U.S. peace moves.

text.p: Two Arab suicide bombers killed 11 people in a crowded Jerusalem market on Wednesday, setting back fresh U.S. efforts to resolve an Israel-PLO peace crisis that has now deepened.

"The slaughter was aimed directly at innocent Israelis, and make no mistake, it was also aimed at the majority of Israelis, Palestinians and Arabs who want a lasting and just peace," U.S. President Bill Clinton told reporters at the White House.

Clinton said a visit to the region by U.S. mediator Dennis Ross, who had been expected to present new ideas on ending a peacemaking deadlock over Israeli settlement building, was being postponed to allow a period of mourning in the Jewish state.

Israel clamped a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanded Palestinian President Yasser Arafat crack down on Moslem militants in the wake of the deadliest single attack on Israelis since March 1996.

"We expect the Palestinian Authority and its leader to begin to fight terror as they are committed to, as they haven't done until today, that they will take all the steps required against these terrorists and their operators who roam free," he told a news conference after visiting wounded in hospital.
"We aren't ready to accept that murderous acts will be part of our daily lives every few weeks and months and we will await suitable steps," Netanyahu said.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the blasts in Jewish west Jerusalem's main Mahane Yehuda market.
The European Union, which has been mediating between Israel and the Palestinians, strongly condemned the attack and urged Israelis not to let it derail the peace process.

"The European Union presidency calls on the government and people of Israel not to be provoked by those who want to torpedo peace," Luxembourg Foreign Minister Jacques Poos said in a statement on behalf of the 15-nation bloc.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan called the bombings "abominable and unfortunate" and appealed to both sides to return to the negotiating table.

Annan recalled telling Netanyahu in a telephone conversation on Monday that he was encouraged by his suspension of construction of a controversial housing project in an Arab neighbourhood in East Jerusalem.
"And so I am disappointed that at a crucial time when we were just on the verge of getting the talks back on track that this should happen," Annan said.
It was Netanyahu's decision in March to plough ahead with another project, the construction of a 6,500-home Jewish settlement on the outskirts of East Jerusalem, that plunged peacemaking into crisis.
France and Germany coupled their condemnations of the bombings with appeals not to let the attacks stop the drive for peace.
"Only the resumption of the peace process, which is necessary and urgent, can open the way to a future for all peoples of the region," French President Jacques Chirac said in a letter to Netanyahu.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel called the attack a "cowardly act", saying in a letter to Israeli counterpart David Levy that "we should not allow the originators and perpetrators to succeed in their aim of destroying the peace process".
Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan said the world and the Palestinian Authority would have to realise "that it is either violence and terrorism or a peace process".
Bar-Illan said if the Authority, in charge of parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, did not wage a "real war" against terrorism, "we will not be able to advance in the peace process".
Arafat telephoned Netanyahu to express his condolences, but the Israeli leader, in a "very tough conversation" said that expressing sorrow was not enough, the prime minister's spokesman said.
Senior Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said both sides had suffered at the hands of opponents of peace.
"The answer should be the strong message that they will not win, extremists on both sides. People who commit terror will not win and the peace process must continue," he said.
